sweep_summary: Mixtepec Zapotec (mixt1426) is not in the catalog. The single keyword-matched bibliography item, Dilley, Shattuck-Hufnagel & Ostendorf 1996 (J. Phonetics 24), is a Glottolog misattribution: its own record flags the zpm tag as a 'computerized assignment from "glottalization"', and the abstract shows an English FM-radio-news corpus study; irrelevant, priority none. The best first-hand stress statement read is Antonio Ramos 2007 (CIESAS MA thesis on San Pedro Mixtepec Zapotec, on file), sec. 5.4 p. 139: all monosyllabic roots are stressed, compounds stress the last syllable, vowel enclitics are unstressed; his 2015 doctoral grammar (pp. 185-186) restates this as trochaic root+clitic feet and iambic N+N compound feet. 2001 36-page sketch (medium priority; Wayback captures empty, IA CDX offline), Reeck 1991 dictionary (low), Nelson 2004 UTA thesis (UTA repository behind Cloudflare). new_statements.quote: La vocal elidida en este zapoteco es la vocal átona, por ello en las raíces monosilábicas existentes siempre encontraremos sílabas con la vocal tónica; como no hay contraste entre átonas y tónicas en raíces monosilábicas, no emplearemos el acento gráfico ya que todas las raíces monosilábicas son tónicas. El acento en palabras bimorfémicas (y bisilábicas) tampoco lo marcamos ya que en los compuestos siempre recae en la última sílaba [...] la última sílaba de este tipo de palabras es la que se pronuncia más fuerte; sin embargo cuando la última sílaba no es parte de una raíz léxica, es decir cuando es un clítico como /í/ y /á/ [...] no recibe el acento en la segunda sílaba
new_statements.translation: The vowel elided in this Zapotec is the unstressed vowel, hence in the existing monosyllabic roots we always find syllables with the stressed vowel; since there is no contrast between unstressed and stressed in monosyllabic roots, we do not use a written accent, as all monosyllabic roots are stressed. Nor do we mark stress in bimorphemic (and disyllabic) words, since in compounds it always falls on the last syllable [...] the last syllable of this type of word is the one pronounced most strongly; however, when the last syllable is not part of a lexical root, i.e. when it is a clitic such as /í/ and /á/ [...] it does not receive stress on the second syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Roots are (historically reduced to) monosyllables and every root is stressed; native disyllables are compounds of two roots, and there stress falls on the final syllable (final root); vowel enclitics (=i 'there', =a 3INAN etc.) never take stress, so root+clitic words are stressed on the root (first syllable). I.e. stress on the last root syllable of the word — root-final/word-final within the lexical word, clitics excluded.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Fn. 36 (p. 118): syntactic combinations of two roots, unlike compounds, keep 'acento fonológico en las dos raíces' (each root stressed).
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel enclitics /=i/, /=a/ are unstressed, short, and always high-toned (e.g. /biep=i/ 'sube allí', /bdob=a/ 'quítalo' stressed on first syllable); phonologically eroded roots such as /ie/ < /nie/ 'verde', /ieʼn/ 'pequeño' in second position DO take stress because they are still lexical roots. TAM prefixes are non-syllabic/unstressed (roots monosyllabic). The 2015 doctoral thesis (pp. 186, 196, 198) recasts this as root+clitic = trochaic foot, N+N compound = iambic foot with moraic reduction of the first root.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word = root(+root); clitics outside the phonological word per 2015: p. 184-185, 196). Language is tonal (5 tones, 2015 ch. 4); stress is described as non-contrastive intensity accent. Citation/isolation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Antonio Ramos theses describe the Zapotec of San Pedro Mixtepec (Dto. Miahuatlán), Glottolog dialect sanp1262 'San Pedro Mixtepec Zapoteco' under mixt1426; the ISO/Ethnologue reference variety is neighbouring San Juan Mixtepec (sanj1288, 5 km away). The author (2015: pp. 32-33) says the two towns differ lexically and tonally (San Pedro has a high-rising tone San Juan lacks; falling tone is non-lexical in San Pedro but lexical in San Juan); no statement that stress placement differs.

new_statements.quote: La vocal elidida en este zapoteco es la vocal átona, por ello en las raíces monosilábicas existentes siempre encontraremos sílabas con la vocal tónica; como no hay contraste entre átonas y tónicas en raíces monosilábicas, no emplearemos el acento gráfico ya que todas las raíces monosilábicas son tónicas. El acento en palabras bimorfémicas (y bisilábicas) tampoco lo marcamos ya que en los compuestos siempre recae en la última sílaba como se observa en la tabla (89).
new_statements.translation: The vowel elided in this Zapotec is the unstressed vowel, so in the existing monosyllabic roots we will always find syllables with the stressed vowel; since there is no contrast between unstressed and stressed in monosyllabic roots, we will not use the written accent, because all monosyllabic roots are stressed. Nor do we mark stress in bimorphemic (and bisyllabic) words, because in compounds it always falls on the last syllable, as seen in Table 89.
new_statements.citation: Antonio Ramos, Pafnuncio. 2007. Las propiedades fonológicas y morfofonológicas del zapoteco de San Pedro Mixtepec, Miahuatlán, Oaxaca. Tesis de maestría, CIESAS, México D.F.
new_statements.locator: sec. 5.4, p. 139 (text layer lines ~5019-5041; page fixed by footers 138/139); corroborated by fn. 36 p. 118 and conclusion 6 p. 226; and by Antonio Ramos 2015 pp. 185-186
new_statements.reading: Stress is root-bound: San Pedro Mixtepec Zapotec words are overwhelmingly monosyllabic roots, each stressed; in root+enclitic words (biep=i, bdob=a) the clitic syllable is unstressed and short, so stress is on the first (root) syllable; in N+N compounds stress falls on the final syllable (the second root). Antonio Ramos 2015 recasts this as trochaic feet for root+clitic (heavy-light) and iambic feet for compounds (light-heavy). The language also has five lexical tones. Caveat: this describes the San Pedro Mixtepec dialect (Glottolog sanp1262 under mixt1426); the ISO-reference San Juan Mixtepec variety has no first-hand stress statement read (Hunn et al. 2001 sketch and Reeck 1991 dictionary not located).

sources.locator: sec. 3.4, pp. 185-186 and p. 197 (word-minimality and foot structure); conclusions p. ~486
sources.note: No section headed 'acento'; prosody is recast in moraic/foot terms consistent with the 2007 thesis: minimal word = one foot (bimoraic monosyllable); root + vowel clitic = trochaic foot (heavy-light, strong element on the root); N+N compound = iambic foot (light-heavy, strong element on the final root, first root's fortis coda de-moraified). Defines foot as 'unidad rítmica mínima... que contrasta un elemento fuerte con uno débil' (p. 184). Corroborates 2007 (root-stress; compounds final).

sources.note: San Pedro Mixtepec Zapotec (sanp1262) is near-monosyllabic (historical loss of the unstressed vowel); every monosyllabic root is stressed. In bisyllabic N+N compounds stress falls on the last syllable (giS='til 'pan', Zob='ze 'maíz', gig='be/ 'río'; Tabla 89). When the second syllable is a vowel enclitic (/=i/, /=a/: biep+i 'sube allí', bdob+a 'quítalo') it is NOT stressed and its vowel is short (always high tone). Fn. 36 p. 118: compounds are bisyllabic with the last syllable stressed, whereas syntactic combinations carry phonological stress on both roots. Conclusion 6 p. 226 restates: monos…

sources.note: Sec. 5.4 'Acento de intensidad...' pp. 137-139: the language lost its historical unstressed (post-tonic) vowel, so all monosyllabic roots are stressed (no tonic/atonic contrast); in disyllabic compounds stress always falls on the last syllable ('la que se pronuncia más fuerte'); vowel enclitics (=i, =a) are not stressed and have a short vowel with high tone; eroded roots like /ie/ 'verde' in second position do take stress. Fn. 36 p. 118: compounds have final-syllable stress vs. syntactic phrases with stress on both roots. Conclusion 6, p. 226 restates.
